questions.q: Why does this lesson explicitly say its Cython code examples were not compiled or benchmarked?
options: Because Cython code is always slower than Numba and not worth running
Because this environment has no C/C++ compiler installed, so .pyx files cannot actually be built here
Because Cython requires an internet connection to run
Because the examples contain intentional bugs
questions.explain: The lesson states directly that no C compiler (cl.exe or gcc) is available in this environment, so .pyx files can't be compiled or benchmarked -- the examples are shown as illustrative, syntactically correct Cython to compile on a machine with a real toolchain.

questions.q: What is the key difference between `cdef` and `cpdef` for a function definition?
options: `cdef` and `cpdef` are identical; the names are just stylistic preference
`cdef` compiles to a pure C function callable only from other Cython code, while `cpdef` also generates a Python-callable wrapper
`cpdef` is only valid inside a setup.py file
`cdef` can only be used for variables, never for functions
questions.explain: A `cdef` function is fast but not visible to plain Python callers; `cpdef` provides both the fast C-level entry point and a Python-callable wrapper, at a small overhead cost for that wrapper.

questions.q: What does a typed memoryview like `double[:]` give Cython code?
options: A way to store strings efficiently
A C-level view directly onto a buffer (such as a NumPy array's memory), avoiding Python-level indexing overhead on each access
Automatic parallelization across CPU cores
A way to avoid writing a setup.py file
questions.explain: A typed memoryview gives Cython a fast, direct, C-level view onto the underlying memory of a buffer like a NumPy array, which is what lets indexing operations skip Python's per-element object overhead.

questions.q: How does Cython's compilation model differ from Numba's, as described in this lesson?
options: They are identical: both compile on first call at runtime

Cython requires an ahead-of-time build step (e.g. `cythonize` + `setup.py build_ext`) before the module can be imported; Numba's `@njit` compiles lazily the first time the function is called at runtime
Numba requires a build step and Cython does not
Neither one requires any compilation
questions.explain: Cython .pyx files must be compiled into a real extension module before import, with no runtime JIT step, while Numba's @njit compiles the first time a decorated function is actually called.

questions.q: According to this lesson, when should you reach for Cython instead of Numba?
options: Always -- Cython is strictly faster in every case
Only when working exclusively with pandas DataFrames
When you need capabilities nopython mode doesn't support, such as wrapping a C/C++ library or working with arbitrary Python objects in a hot loop, not as a default first choice over Numba
Never -- Cython is deprecated in favor of Numba
questions.explain: The lesson recommends starting with vectorization, then Numba for array/loop-shaped numeric code, and reaching for Cython specifically when Numba's restrictions -- not just raw speed -- are the actual blocker.
